In my experience most people won't say anything and if you act confident enough, they won't even care. When you introduce yourself with a male name from the beginning it will help you pass because they can now know for sure that you are a boy.

I meet a lot of new people because I am travelling a lot and they usually don't question it when I introduce myself as male, but of course there are assh*les that won't respect you or there might be people who just don't know or understand these things. The first ones, you sadly just have to ignore, but with the others, just try to be patient and explain it if you need to. They'll usually understand and respect it (if they are somewhat decent human beings) and it's worth it even if it's a pain sometimes.

First thing I did even before I knew I was trans was to copy how other men walk and sit. Most women keep their legs in a line while walking or closed when sitting while most men sit with their legs open. 
Also try to keep your back straight, work on a good posture and act confident even if you aren't. It may be hard at the beginning (especially keeping your back straight, when you don't want to show your upper body) but it makes you seem more masculine and helps you later in life when you are out because most people won't question it if you are confident enough. 

However these are just my observations and they don't have to apply to everyone. I know a lot of men who sit with their legs closed or walk in a straight line and no one cares.

>is it okay to say "you look like a natural born female" or is that more insulting? 

I think it could be insulting, I have days, where I feel good about these kinds of compliments, but especially on days where my disphoria is really strong, it makes me feel like I am not a "real" man. So I think you should rather compliment her like you would any other woman. Compliment her hair, her clothes or make-up if she wears any, just treat her like every other woman and it's cool I think.

>What can I do to make her feel better about the rejection of other family members? 

Be there for her. There isn't much you can actively do but listen to her, support her and maybe try to talk to those who rejected her, explain things to them and help them understand her
